Yeah sorry about that. This is a software defined radio based on a hangar at Orcas island, receiving the entire airband, channelizing it into over 700 channels, and then demodulating the channels and playing whatever is sent provided it's voice. It also transcribes using a voice model and an LLM parses the output and attempts to create cards on the right hand side. It's also trying to detect simulcasts and remove the duplicate transmissions. Hope that helps explain it. It's also archiving everything so you can listen to old transmissions. Right now I'm working to keep the server up. Thanks HN. :-) For context, I'm a pilot based at KORS and a nerd.

mmaunder · Nov 13, 2026

Hi all. Thanks for the interest. I'm going to post an impromptu blog post here just explaining what this is. The rather unfortunate ground stop today made this unexpectedly useful with the pilots here on Orcas just to get a sense of the chatter in our airspace re the situation.

This is an ETTUS B210 attached to a dual 4090 box. It's a polyphase channelizer that takes the entire airband, channelizes it using cuda code on GPU, demodulates it, detects transmissions, throws away data tx and then feeds the tx through a voice model I created for transcription. A separate LLM reads the transcriptions to create a situational awareness picture of the airspace.

I'm interested in open sourcing this and making it available for folks who can run an ETTUS B210 or high quality SDR with enoguh bandwidth and a local GPU machine, so that we can cover more airpsace.

This was born out of an incident we had not too long ago where a pilot around KORS (based at Friday Harbor) lost the engine in his 172, and put it in the water in front of a ferry and was picked up by the ferry. We're a pretty close bunch on Orcas Island and we only heard about it days later via social media. That felt completely unacceptable, and I set out to create a radio that could monitor everything in real-time, all the time, and alert on emergencies. That has extended to transcribing and creating situational awareness for a chunk of airspace.

I'm an IFR pilot. I fly a T206H regularly in IMC around here and I'm a ground instructor. You can email me at mark@defiant.com or find me on x at mmaunder if you'd like to connect. I'm particularly interested in hearing from folks who can run a station on their own hardware and are under bravo or a charlie or even just somewhere interesting re airspace.

amluto · Nov 14, 2026

I would expect that the hardware involved is massive overkill.

The Ettus SDRs are very nice and are marked up enormously over the BOM cost. You’re paying for an integrated, supported system, with good engineering, not for the parts. These days, for this particular use, you could probably build your own direct (no downconversion) receiver with a decent filter and, say, a 400MSPS DAC. (This was not a thing at any reasonable price point 15 years ago when I last played with this stuff.) Or you can buy or build a little mixer and choose an appropriate LO frequency and use a much cheaper DAC. Or you can buy a cheaper SDR.

~15 years ago I amused myself for about an hour using a USRP (older Ettus gear) and MATLAB to do more or less this but for regular FM radio, one channel at a time, on a decent laptop of the era. The processing power needed to channelize and demodulate a few channels from I/Q data is very, very low. Even coming up with some kind of optimal demodulation scheme wouldn’t use many cycles. (Although I suspect that there is more space to try to jointly optimize demodulation and transcription with FM than with AM.)

It would be a fun project to try to kludge up an ESP32 of some sort to do this. The tricky bit would be that the WiFi/BT hardware doesn’t go to DC.

mmaunder · Nov 13, 2026

Ah this is such a hot debate in the community. Yes it's straight up AM simplex and the argument for is: With AM when you step on another tx it screeches. Also pilots can hear pilots to improve situational awareness vs duplex which would have pilots only hearing ATC. Huge legacy fleet of aircraft. Cost to upgrade anything in a certified aircraft. There are so many arguments for digital though. it's a tough one.

keito · Nov 13, 2026

Also, the recordings you hear online will often be more garbled (weaker signal) than what you hear in the cockpit or what ATC hears, because (1) in the air you have clear line of sight to the ground transmitter and to other planes, and (2) ATC has receivers that are designed to be able to cover the area they're controlling.

jaggederest · Nov 13, 2026

The counterpoint to that is that for the same SNR where you're at barely (or not at all) audible or garbled on analog, you have absolutely clear digital audio.

teravor · Nov 14, 2026

with digital you can utilize the bandwidth much better thanks to compression.

you can also load up on error correction to such an extent that what would have been completely garbled analog audio would instead result in crystal clear digital.

and this ignores the potential for a secondary ultra low bandwidth transcription text stream that would play back with TTS if all else fails.

the real reason this hasn't happened is backward compatibility hell and regulation up the wazoo. there isn't going to be much money to be made in pioneering this, a tiny startup that may wish to serve this tiny market would take one look at the regulation and nope out.

npunt · Nov 14, 2026

There's also the accessibility case, as its quite common for people to have wildly different abilities in auditory discrimination, including auditory processing disorders. That's probably a big reason why people have such differences of opinion of how bad they perceive the problem to be. Its likely such a selective pressure on the industry that a number of people just don't stick around because of it, so the industry likely undercounts it.

Any kind of auditory discrimination challenge someone has will lead to much higher cognitive load to interpret noisy transmissions. That cognitive load is a resource that could be better spent on other flight instruments and crisis situations.

Putting a design lens on, someone with APD an extreme user who, if properly made accessible to, would wind up improving everyone's experience not just their own.

I wonder if a switch to digital could keep transmitting on analog for legacy needs while having a second digital system be the primary one used.
